```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(RdistNN)
set.seed(3)
```

## Choose an extension point

Most extensions replace one part of the estimation pipeline:

| Goal | Extension |
|---|---|
| Change closeness or observation ordering | Distance or ranking provider |
| Change the weight profile for given ranks | Rank-weight rule |
| Change the order `s` for a given `(n, kx, k)` | Tuning specification |
| Evaluate another kernel on data subsets | Score |
| Reuse external distances, orders or ranks | `weights_matrix(ranking = ...)` |

Use `as_distance()`, `as_rank_weight()` or `as_score()` for a simple function.
Their `new_*()` counterparts support batch evaluation, setup context and
parameter-aware score derivatives.

For kernel-order specifications, use [Kernel-order tuning](kernel-order-tuning.html).
For result classes and reporting conventions, use [Notation and conventions](notation-and-conventions.html).

## Custom distances

### Quick Prototype With `as_distance()`

Use `as_distance()` when a simple function `(X, x0, ctx) -> numeric(n)` is
enough.

```{r distance-simple}
# L-infinity distance
linf <- as_distance(
  function(X, x0, ctx = NULL) {
    apply(abs(X - matrix(x0, nrow(X), ncol(X), byrow = TRUE)), 1L, max)
  },
  name = "linf"
)

register_distance("linf", linf)
distance_names()
```

You can test the distance directly before registering it:

```{r distance-eval}
X <- matrix(rnorm(40), 20, 2)
x0 <- c(0, 0)

distance_eval(linf, X, x0)
dim(distance_eval_batch(linf, X[1L, , drop = FALSE], rbind(x0, x0)))
```

### Reusable Distance With `new_distance()`, `setup()`, and `eval_batch()`

Use `new_distance()` when you want to precompute context once on `X` and reuse
it across many targets.

```{r distance-batch}
scaled_l2 <- new_distance(
  name = "scaled_l2_demo",
  setup = function(X) {
    scale <- apply(X, 2L, stats::sd)
    scale[!is.finite(scale) | scale <= 0] <- 1
    list(scale = scale)
  },
  eval_batch = function(X, X0, ctx) {
    D <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(X0)), function(j) {
      delta <- sweep(X, 2L, X0[j, ], "-")
      sqrt(rowSums(sweep(delta, 2L, ctx$scale, "/")^2))
    }, numeric(nrow(X)))
    matrix(D, nrow = nrow(X), ncol = nrow(X0))
  }
)

X <- matrix(rnorm(80), 40, 2)
X0 <- matrix(rnorm(12), 6, 2)

ctx_dist <- scaled_l2$setup(X)
D <- distance_eval_batch(scaled_l2, X, X0, ctx = ctx_dist)
dim(D)
```

Batch distances have shape `n x m`, including a single observation or target.
A custom `eval_batch()` must return an actual matrix with those dimensions.
Scalar-only specs use the shared batch evaluator, which assembles the matrix
without dropping singleton dimensions. With `ctx = NULL`, distance-side
`setup(X)` runs once per batch, including calls through `weights_matrix()`.
Pass a fitted context explicitly to reuse it across calls.

## Custom rank weights

Rank weights only see integer ranks, not raw distances. Rank `1` means "closest
observation," rank `2` means "second closest," and so on.

That separation is useful because you can change the localization profile
without changing the ranking logic.

### Quick Prototype With `as_rank_weight()`

```{r rank-simple}
rw_inv <- as_rank_weight(
  function(ranks, ctx = NULL) {
    w <- 1 / as.numeric(ranks)
    w / sum(w)
  },
  name = "inv_rank"
)

register_rank_weight("inv_rank", rw_inv)
rank_weight_names()
dim(rank_weight_eval_batch(rw_inv, matrix(1L, nrow = 1L, ncol = 2L)))
```

### A Compact-Support Rule

This example keeps only the first `m` closest observations in rank order. That
is a generic finite-support rule. It is not the same thing as exact DNN.

```{r rank-support}
make_top_m <- function(m) {
  if (length(m) != 1L || !is.numeric(m) || !is.finite(m) || m < 1 || m != floor(m)) {
    stop("`m` must be a positive integer.", call. = FALSE)
  }

  as_rank_weight(
    function(ranks) {
      keep <- as.numeric(ranks <= m)
      keep / sum(keep)
    },
    name = paste0("top_", m)
  )
}

rw_top10 <- make_top_m(10L)
```

`rank_weight_eval()` evaluates the supplied rank rule without distance groups.
When that rule is passed to `weights_matrix()` with distances available, the
localization layer averages its assigned weights within exact represented
selected-metric distance groups, separately for each target. This includes
signed or unnormalized rules and zero entries beyond nominal support. A support
boundary inside a group can therefore give nonzero observation weights beyond
the original cutoff. Custom rankers remain responsible for their supplied
permutations; bare ranks/orders do not infer groups, while retained `dx` enables
distance grouping. See
[DNN weights and ranks](dnn-weights.html#exact-distance-ties) for the
grouping rule, deletion redistribution and theory warning.

### Batched Rank Weights and Shared `ctx`

For performance, prefer `eval_batch()` once the prototype is stable.
Scalar-only rules are evaluated and validated one target at a time; their
batch output stays `n x m` even when either dimension is one. A custom batch
callback must itself return an `n x m` matrix.

```{r rank-batch}
rw_exp <- new_rank_weight(
  name = "exp_decay",
  eval_batch = function(R, ctx = NULL) {
    lambda <- if (is.null(ctx) || is.null(ctx$lambda)) 0.25 else ctx$lambda
    W <- exp(-lambda * (R - 1L))
    sweep(W, 2L, colSums(W), "/")
  }
)

R <- cbind(1:5, c(2L, 1L, 3L, 4L, 5L))
rank_weight_eval_batch(rw_exp, R, ctx = list(lambda = 0.5))
```

At the top level, `weights_matrix()` passes any supplied `ctx` through to both
the ranking and weight evaluators. If both sides need context, build one shared
list.

`weights_matrix()` does not call rank-weight-side `setup()` automatically.
Close over fixed parameters in the constructor, or build and pass a shared
`ctx` when both the ranking and weights need context.

## Combine ranking and weights

`weights_matrix()` is the main modular entry point. The `ranking` argument can
be:

- a distance spec or registered distance name;
- a function `(X, X0, ctx)` that returns `dx`, `ord`, or `ranks`;
- a precomputed list with `dx`, `ord`, or `ranks`;
- a ranks matrix directly.

That makes it the right place to integrate custom ranking code, precomputed
distances, or external nearest-neighbor engines.

```{r weights-matrix}
n <- 80
p <- 2
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
X0 <- matrix(rnorm(4 * p), 4, p)

# If only the distance needs setup, leave ctx = NULL and let the distance
# auto-setup path run.
out1 <- weights_matrix(
  X = X,
  X0 = X0,
  ranking = scaled_l2,
  weight = rw_top10,
  return = c("W", "dx", "ord", "ranks")
)

# If both the distance and the weight need context, build one shared list.
ctx_both <- c(scaled_l2$setup(X), list(lambda = 0.35))
out2 <- weights_matrix(
  X = X,
  X0 = X0,
  ranking = scaled_l2,
  weight = rw_exp,
  ctx = ctx_both,
  return = c("W", "dx", "ord", "ranks")
)

dim(out2$W)
```

For debugging custom ranking behavior, request the intermediate objects:

```{r weights-debug}
lapply(out2[c("dx", "ord", "ranks", "W")], function(x) head(x[, 1L]))
```

## Custom scores

The score layer is separate from localization. A score describes what happens
once a subset of observations has been selected.

### Quick Prototype With `as_score()`

Use `as_score()` for a simple kernel with fixed order `s`.
Each scalar callback must return one finite numeric value per subset. Logical
values and multiple values are rejected before the batch output is assembled.

```{r score-simple}
sc_avg2 <- as_score(
  function(idxs, data, ctx = NULL, rng = NULL) {
    mean(data$Y[idxs])
  },
  s = 2L,
  name = "avg2"
)

register_score("avg2", sc_avg2)
list_scores()

df <- data.frame(Y = rnorm(10))
subs <- rbind(c(1L, 2L), c(4L, 8L), c(3L, 9L))
score_eval_batch(sc_avg2, subs = subs, data = df)
```

### Reusable Score With `new_score()` and `setup()`

Use `setup()` when the score repeatedly accesses the same data columns or
transformed objects.

```{r score-setup}
sc_pair_gap <- new_score(
  name = "pair_gap_sq",
  order = 2L,
  setup = function(data, ...) list(y = as.numeric(data$Y)),
  eval_batch = function(subs, data, ctx, rng = NULL) {
    (ctx$y[subs[, 1L]] - ctx$y[subs[, 2L]])^2
  }
)

df <- data.frame(Y = rnorm(10))
ctx_score <- score_setup(sc_pair_gap, df)
subs <- rbind(c(1L, 2L), c(2L, 5L), c(3L, 4L))

score_eval_batch(sc_pair_gap, subs, data = df, ctx = ctx_score)
```

### Parameter-Aware Scores And Derivatives With `score_diff_path()`

If your score depends on a parameter vector, implement `eval_param` or an
`eval` that accepts `theta`, then use `score_diff_path()` to get reusable value
and gradient closures.
An analytic batch gradient must be a two-dimensional `K x p` matrix for `K`
subsets and `p` parameters. When `p = 1`, a numeric vector of length `K` is
also accepted and converted to that matrix; higher-dimensional arrays are
rejected.

```{r score-diff}
sc_affine <- new_score(
  name = "affine_order1",
  order = 1L,
  eval_param = function(idxs, data, theta, ctx, rng = NULL) {
    theta[1] * data$Y[idxs] + theta[2]
  },
  grad = function(idxs, data, theta, ctx, rng = NULL) {
    c(data$Y[idxs], 1)
  }
)

df <- data.frame(Y = c(1, 2, 4))
path <- score_diff_path(sc_affine, data = df, method = "auto")

path$value(2L, theta = c(0.5, 1))
path$grad(2L, theta = c(0.5, 1))
```

`score_diff_path()` evaluates its `data` argument when the path is created.
Rebinding `df` later does not change the data used by this path. Custom
closures, environments and external pointers can still contain mutable state;
their authors remain responsible for reproducible evaluations.

If you do not provide an analytic gradient, `score_diff_path(..., method = "fd")`
uses finite differences based on `eval_param` / `eval_param_batch`.

## A minimal estimator

The modular API is meant to let you assemble your own localized estimators
without rewriting the whole package. A minimal pattern is:

```{r estimator-pattern}
my_local_mean <- function(X, x0, y, ranking = "l2", weight) {
  W <- weights_matrix(
    X = X,
    x0 = x0,
    ranking = ranking,
    weight = weight,
    return = "W"
  )$W[, 1L]

  sum(W * y)
}

my_local_mean(X, x0 = X0[1, ], y = X[, 1], weight = rw_top10)
```

For more complicated estimators, replace the scalar `y` contribution with your
own score or estimating equation.

## Check an extension

Test the evaluator on a small dataset before registering its name. Check its
output shape and finite values, and request `W`, `dx`, `ord` and `ranks` to
inspect the weighting pipeline. Specs receive ranks rather than raw distances;
when both ranking and weighting need setup, pass an explicit shared `ctx`.

Custom estimators need their own statistical justification. The examples here
show software composition; the [paper](https://jakobjuergens.com/research/#orthogonal-inference-conditional-z)
and its references give the background for the package's estimators.
